lesson.subtitle: Lesson 2 -- The Small Print

lesson.grammar_point: obligation and permission with must, have to and be allowed to

listenings.text: I have worked on a hotel front desk for nine years, and there are three lines on the booking page that nobody reads. The first one is the deposit. Almost every hotel takes a deposit when you book, and the money is not a payment, it is a hold. You get it back, but you get it back in ten working days, not on the day you leave. The second line is the fee for changing the date. Guests always tell me they cancelled, so they should get everything back. That is only true on a flexible rate. On the cheap rate, the room is non-refundable, and the word non-refundable means what it says. The third line is the one that costs people the most money, and it is the check-in time. If you land at six in the morning, your room is not ready at six. You are allowed to leave your bags with us free of charge, and most people do not know that.

Here is the question we get every week on this programme. Should you book the cheap rate or the flexible one? Look at the difference in price first. If the flexible rate costs fifteen per cent more, you are buying insurance, and the question is simply whether the trip is likely to change. A family holiday booked eleven months in advance is not the same as a work trip next Tuesday. The second thing to check is what the word refund actually means on that page. Some companies give you money; a lot of them give you a voucher, and a voucher is not a refund. And the third thing, which almost nobody does: save the confirmation e-mail as a file, not as an e-mail. If you have to argue at a desk in another country, the proof you can show on a screen in five seconds is worth more than the proof you have to look for.

paras: Two women booked the same room in the same hotel, on the same afternoon, for the same week in October. One of them paid four hundred dollars and the other paid four hundred and sixty. They both got the same bed and the same view. Six weeks later one of them changed her dates and lost everything, and the other one changed her dates and paid nothing.

The difference was one line on the booking page, and neither of them read it. The cheaper rate said non-refundable, which means the hotel keeps the money even if you never arrive. The more expensive rate said free cancellation until seventy-two hours before check-in. The sixty dollars were not a better room. They were insurance, and one of the two women bought it without knowing.

The rest of the page is short, and it is the same in most hotels. Guests have to show a photo ID at check-in, and they have to leave a deposit on a card. The deposit is not a payment: the hotel holds it and releases it after you leave, usually in ten working days. Children under twelve are allowed to stay in the room free of charge, but the hotel has to know they are coming, because the fire rules count people, not beds.

And there is one line that costs travellers more time than money. Check-in is at three in the afternoon. If your flight lands at six in the morning, the room is not ready, and no amount of arguing at the desk changes that. What you are allowed to do is leave your bags with the hotel, free of charge, and come back at three. Most people never ask, because the line is at the bottom of a page nobody reads.
reading.source: Written for this lesson, from the standard terms of a mid-range hotel booking page.

choices: To advise travellers never to book the cheaper rate.
To show what the booking page actually promises, and what the two rates really buy.
To explain how hotels decide the price of a room in October.

items: The two women got different rooms for the different prices.
The text says they both got the same bed and the same view; the difference was one line about cancellation.
On a non-refundable rate the hotel keeps the money even if the guest never arrives.
The text says exactly that, and calls the extra sixty dollars insurance.
The deposit is part of the payment for the room.
The text says the deposit is not a payment: the hotel holds it and releases it after you leave.
A hotel does not need to know that a child is coming, as long as the child is under twelve.
The text says the hotel has to know, because the fire rules count people, not beds.
A guest who lands at six in the morning can ask the hotel to keep the bags at no cost.
The text says you are allowed to leave your bags free of charge and come back at three.

items.situation: The receptionist asks for something before she gives you the key. Say what you have, and say the rule.
tips: I have my passport here. Guests have to show a photo ID at check-in.
Watch the form: must show and have to show, never must to show.

items.situation: You land at six in the morning and the room is not ready. Ask for what the page already promises you.
tips: Am I allowed to leave my bags here until three?
Are we allowed to, never Are we allowed take.

items.situation: Somebody tells you to print the confirmation. Answer, and say why not.
tips: I do not have to print it. The e-mail on my phone is the proof of the reservation.
Do not have to means there is no obligation. It does not mean it is forbidden.

items.situation: A friend booked the non-refundable rate and wants to change the date. Tell her what she can and cannot do.
tips: You are not allowed to change it free of charge, so you have to pay a fee.
Are not allowed to and must not both work here. Do not have to would be wrong.

items.situation: Say one rule of your own consulting room to a patient who speaks no Portuguese.
tips: Patients have to arrive ten minutes early, and they must not eat before the appointment.
Use have to for the rule that comes from outside, must for the rule that is yours.

items.situation: Say one thing that was obligatory on your last trip, in the past.
tips: We had to pay a fee to change the date.
There is no musted. The past of must and have to is had to.
